en: Composed by the Śramaṇa Zhànrán of Bīlíng during the Táng Dynasty.
Chapter Two: Explaining the Names. Now, the establishment of names varies; as the Mahāyāna Sūtra states:
"Some have causes and conditions, such as Maudgalyāyana and others; some lack causes and conditions, such as the peach and plum trees."
And so forth.
Nirvana is also like this;
there is no causal basis for forcibly establishing a name for it.
It is the same with śamatha and vipaśyanā; they are given the provisional names "śamatha" and "vipaśyanā.
That which is without cause is called "having a cause";
these designations are established according to the capacities of sentient beings for their sake.
Furthermore, supramundane designations are established based upon mundane designations;
therefore, the noble ones first establish mundane names as a skillful means for establishing supramundane names.
Yet these worldly names are fundamentally supramundane;
as the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states:
"All worldly names originate from the Buddha's scriptures."
Therefore, we know that various names are established based on the principles of phenomena (*dharmatā*);
since the name is the principle of the phenomenon, the principle likewise depends upon the name.
Thus, one employs sublime names as a provisional means to elucidate sublime principles. As Zhuangzi said:
Yet the world prizes words and transmitted books, which are not worthy of such esteem.
Since Zhuangzi has already used words to transmit his books, Zhuangzi himself is not inherently worthy of being prized. Laozi said:
To know is not to speak; to speak is not to know.
Thus, when Laozi speaks, it is the same as not knowing.
His intention is to bring about a state where there is no speaking in the world.
You alone have voiced your own words;
you did not expect that, by means of these very words, you would instead refute yourself and the world of men.
You are now beset by these words of self-refutation.
Yet they secretly reject it, mistakenly believing that [the former] has attained [the truth]; this is an extreme error.
Now, it is not so: having caught the rabbit by means of the snare, one discards the snare once the task is done.
If one asks what a net lacks, it is not said to be a rabbit.
Is this not what is meant by "liberation through words"?
Establishing the names "śamatha" and "vipaśyanā" can be seen as analogous to the distinctions previously made between the extensive and the concise.
It is also called "general and specific.
The two passages, general and specific, illuminate one another.
Therefore, the preceding text states:
The fivefold summary arises within the tenfold detailed exposition.
Furthermore, the preceding summary and the subsequent detail are for the purpose of explaining the meaning,
while the preceding detail and the subsequent summary are for the purpose of retention.
Now, I shall elaborate upon the previous summary so that the meaning may be easily understood.
This is done because there are two types of people— those of sharp and dull faculties— which differ from one another,
as described in the thirty-first fascicle of the Mahāyāna Sūtra.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Be careful not to preach the Dharma extensively for those of sharp faculties,
nor to preach it in brief for those of dull faculties."
Śāriputra said, "I spoke out of compassion, not because my faculties and powers were complete.
The Buddha said:
The extensive and abbreviated teachings of the Dharma are not within the knowledge of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Although the sutra, for the purpose of accommodating various capacities, uses the disparagement of Śāriputra as its pretext,
the present treatise, in its explanation, addresses both types of individuals.
Moreover, the preceding abbreviated text was intended merely to generate understanding;
since that understanding was not yet complete, this extensive treatise is provided.
Furthermore, the meaning of this extensive text is identical to the fivefold profound significance (*pañcavidha-gambhīrārtha*).
The fivefold sequence consists of profound discourses on the essential tenets of the teaching;
the present work, however, bases its practice upon the sutras.
Thus, while that [work] serves as an exegesis of the sutra, this serves to establish contemplation; for this reason, the sequence differs slightly from that [work].
First, the "explanation of names" (śe-ming) indicates the title itself.
Second, the "essence and characteristics" (ti-xiang) reveals the essence.
"Inclusion of phenomena" (she-fa) clarifies only the phenomena subsumed within that essence.
The latter three [categories] of the skillful means clarify the fundamental tenet;
the arousal of the teaching constitutes its function; and the distinction between the partial and the perfect constitutes the judgment of the teachings.

In that explanation of the *Lotus Sūtra*, it is necessary to distinguish the teaching gates throughout the Buddha’s entire life; therefore, the teaching is placed last, while the preceding four [sections] are distinguished first.
This serves to establish contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), for contemplation arises from understanding.
The names and entities, whether partial or complete, all belong to understanding (*jñāna*).
Since practice (*caryā*) is established by virtue of understanding, the "skillful means" (*upāya*) and "correct contemplation" (*samyag-darśana*) follow after understanding.
The beginning of practice serves as the cause, while the end of practice constitutes the fruit.
Therefore, following right contemplation, the fruit and retribution are clarified.
This fundamental principle is for one's own practice, while its application is for the benefit of others.
Because one's own practice is fulfilled, one is able to give rise to the purport of the teaching; this ultimate goal is simply that which is realized by both self and others.
Therefore, when that *Xuánwén* (Profound Text) quotes the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers" (*Shénlì pǐn*) according to the sequence of the teachings,
it is termed "Function, Substance, and Thesis" (*yòng-tǐ-zōng*); however, if it quotes the "Introductory Chapter" (*Xù pǐn*) according to the sequence of practice,
it is termed "Substance, Thesis, and Function" (*tǐ-zōng-yòng*).
The present text properly follows the sequence of practice; however,
because the characteristics of the teachings (*jiaoxiang*) precede the essential tenets (*zong*),
the relationship between the preceding and following sections is as previously explained.
Now, the names are explained.
First, the connection between the preceding and the following is established; this is also the sequence of the underlying intent.
Generally speaking, the preceding section has been concluded.
Furthermore, "departure" refers to that which follows after birth.
It is a path; because its specific tracks and routes have not yet been discussed in detail, it is called the "Great Path" (dàtú).
"Jing" (梗) means rough;
"lue" (略) means general.
This merely provides a rough outline of the main principles.
As previously stated, the general meaning regarding the practice and realization of cause and effect for oneself and others is largely complete.
However, by what definition are these termed "calm abiding" (śamatha) and "insight" (vipaśyanā)?
Therefore, the present text opens this into four sections.
If this explanation were not provided, by what means could one distinguish the function of names and their referents?
Therefore, there are four sections:

the first three correctly clarify the names that serve as the expressive designators (*vācaka*), while the final one establishes the relationship between the expressed referent (*vācya*) and the designator.
Waiting for expression is sequential, while the severance of expression is non-sequential.
To realize difference is merely another name for the severance of relativity.
Regarding the initial "relative," the mutual definition of this and that is called "form" (xiāng).
To regard another in relation to oneself constitutes "dependence," just as "long" and "short" or "large" and "small" mutually receive their names from one another.
As Zhuangzi said:
A person seven feet tall is not considered large,
yet an ant measuring seven inches receives the designation "large.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya-ṭīkā* states:
"Waiting" (pratīkṣā) means "relative dependence" (apekṣā).
When the former is observed in relation to the latter, it is called "past"; when the latter is observed in relation to the former, it is called "future.
Father, son, and brother obtain their names in mutual dependence upon one another.
This can be seen from such examples.
It is judged that the present *Lotus Sūtra* possesses only two excellences,
namely, the "relative" (*dai*) and the "absolute" (*zetsu*).
What is meant by "relative" is that only the coarse is relative to the subtle;
there is nothing further where the subtle is relative to the coarse.
If one regards the traces from the perspective of the source, they may likewise be mutually defined.
If one were to compare vehicle to vehicle, it would be exclusively and unilaterally "wondrous.
Now, regarding the provisional traces (*jia*) and the ultimate principle (*li*) of the *Lotus Sūtra*, we set aside their mutual forms;
therefore, in the *Xuanyan* (Profound Meaning), both the relative (*dai*) and the absolute (*jue*) are termed "wondrous."
Therefore, when comparing the teachings of the various sections, there is both a vertical and a horizontal relationship.
In relation to the preceding four periods, it is called "vertical" (竪); in relation to the three vehicles, it is called "horizontal" (橫).
Since this text follows the intent of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*,
its general exposition of the [four] aspects— such as the name and so forth— is based upon that sūtra. Among these,
"relative" (*pratītya*) refers to the coarse level.
In principle, one should discuss the subtle by waiting upon the coarse;
when all dependencies are severed, that is the subtle.
In principle, one should discuss the subtle by opening up the coarse.
These two are also termed "abandoning the coarse" and "opening up the coarse.
Therefore, in the *Lotus Sūtra*, only these two subtleties are discussed;
there are no further names such as "neither relative nor absolute."
In that [previous] context, for the purpose of classifying the teachings (*p'an-chiao*), both the "relative" (*t'ai*) and the "absolute" (*chüeh*) were equally termed "wondrous.
Now, this relative aspect is judged to be "coarse.
It clarifies only the absolute contemplation (*chüeh-kuan*); since there is no division to which it could be relative, there is no vertical relativity (*shu-t'ai*).
Since there is no teaching that can be expected, it is called "non-dependent.
Therefore, the single state of absolute transcendence serves as the expressive designation.
Although dependent relations are established to manifest this absolute transcendence, [the ultimate meaning remains non-dependent].
Since even "non-existence" does not apply to that which is absolute, what reliance could there be on it?
It is for the purpose of explicating the three virtues that "absolute" is used as a provisional designation;
by borrowing the term "relative," it is judged to be within the realm of discursive thought (*cintya*).
Therefore, it is only when something is absolute and beyond dependence that it can be called "wondrous.
Consequently, although the Buddha-realm following the realm of conceptual thought is indeed wondrous,
because it occupies the very end of the nine realms and is thus collectively categorized as coarse, both are judged accordingly.
This is not what is currently employed.
The same applies to the meanings of "sequential" and "non-sequential";
therefore, the meaning of sequence is simply referred to as the "Vaipulya (Expansive) Gate."
Although it is said that the general and the particular are not employed, yet they are merely termed "resembling the general" and "resembling the particular.
Though it is said that they are not used, this is primarily intended to clarify the inconceivable through the conceivable;
by opening up that which is depended upon, one establishes the capacity for absolute transcendence.
This is precisely the meaning of the "wondrous contemplation" (miaoguan) in the present text.
The same applies to all subsequent meanings explained below regarding the analysis of names (shiming).
Therefore, the analysis of names involves both the relative (dai) and the absolute (jue).

Regarding the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, its sequential and non-sequential aspects, as well as its sixfold categorization of phenomena and fivefold gates of partial and complete teachings, are likewise similar; although there is no formal textual correspondence for direct comparison, they may be discussed in relation to one another.

Furthermore, by borrowing the flavor of the provisional teachings to manifest the perfect and subtle, the ten contemplations for each and every object should be understood as being solely subtle; yet they still rely on the horizontal and vertical modes to manifest that which is neither horizontal nor vertical.
Thus, we know that the text of this entire treatise collectively establishes the Perfect Vehicle and reveals the subtle contemplation that opens up the provisional.
How could one point to a single phrase and claim it to be uniquely profound?
If that were the case, what would distinguish this from merely following the physical form?
Within this, there are four textual sections and two meanings; however, the intent lies solely in one.

There are two [aspects] based on the distinction between the relative and the absolute, yet the intent resides in the absolute. Furthermore, since the object (the supported) is one and the subject (the supporting) is three, they are also said to be one in meaning, because it is the subject that is revealed by the object; thus, the intent is one.
Regarding the three types of cessation (samatha):
although three names are established, these names remain general and comprehensive;

they encompass the three truths (trisatya) without yet distinguishing their relative depths. It is only upon reaching the manifestation of the essence that distinctions of superiority and inferiority are divided according to their respective positions.

The three meanings within contemplation are likewise so. Regarding the phrase "various evil discursive thoughts and the like," the wording resembles that of [the afflictions of] view and thought, yet its meaning is intended as a general exposition.
The citation from the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* is also intended as a general proof.
If one were to borrow the phrasing of the "body and characteristics" (tǐxiàng) to pre-emptively analyze this,
it would mean that the cessation of views and afflictions involves settling the mind upon the ultimate truth (zhēnlǐ). Yet,
the ultimate truth itself is neither something to be settled upon nor something not to be settled upon.
If one quiets the sands of dust and halts the mind upon conventional truth,
conventional truth is neither something to be halted nor not to be halted.
If one quiets ignorance and halts the mind upon the Middle Way, [the same applies].
The Middle Truth is neither cessation nor non-cessation;
thus, there are three types of cessation for each of the Three Truths.
One should understand that the same applies to contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) by analogy.
Therefore, the subsequent text states:
"The first three establish the next three;
the last one possesses all three."
Since the sequence is thus, the same principle applies to the single mind (*ekacitta*).
Next, during the stage of abiding, one contemplates the true principle with the mind as the object;
this is the *Prajñāpāramitā* for entering the principle as taught in the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*, which is general rather than specific, and its meaning is also as previously explained.
Therefore, what is referred to here as "principle" (li) merely denotes the wisdom capable of entering [that principle];
it does not yet denote the principle that is entered.
The same applies to the section on contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Regarding the third section on tranquility (*śamatha*), it says: "The words are common, but the meanings differ.
Here too, it is said that tranquility is clarified by contrast with non-tranquility.
The phrasing is similar to the preceding passage.
In the previous section, "cessation" was contrasted with "non-cessation" and "stopping" with "non-stopping";
now, "ignorance" is contrasted with "dharmatā."
Viewed superficially,
ignorance appears to be non-ceasing and non-still, while the dharma-nature appears to be ceasing and still;
therefore it is said that the words apply to the superior [state], but the meaning is not so.
Ignorance is itself the dharma-nature;
the dharma-nature is itself ignorance.
Their substance is identical while their names differ; they are designated as opposites in relative contrast.
Therefore, it is eternally distinct from the two preceding types of cessation (*śamatha*).
Since the two preceding types cannot be said to be mutually identical, the phrase "now separately concerning the equal" correctly sets forth the characteristics of the third type of cessation.
As for what is meant by "distinct":
the two types of cessation mentioned above belong only to the general category.
To say they belong to the general category means:
Both types of cessation each possess one wisdom and one abandonment.
Regarding the side of abandonment, wisdom exists;
furthermore, with respect to birth and death, the term "abandonment" is established in reference to nirvāṇa.
The limit of wisdom involves cessation and stands outside of mere reasoning;
it is established as the name "wisdom" (jñāna) by way of *prajñā*.
Because it is cessation, it is called "resting," and because it is wisdom, it is called "stopping."
Wisdom is defined in terms of that which can sever, while severance is defined in terms of that which is severed;
therefore, it is said that wisdom and severance together encompass both types of cessation (*śamatha*).
Now, however, this is not the case.
Focusing specifically on the principle of the Truths (satya), this principle is neither subject nor object;
rather, it is simply that because afflictions (kleśa) are present, afflictions are themselves the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
The mutual dependence of the nature of afflictions does not concern the abandonment of wisdom.
Therefore, the third [type of] cessation differs from the preceding two.
Furthermore, while the name of the third cessation is established based on principle (*tattva*), it does not itself constitute a cessation of principle;
the former two cessations rely solely upon wisdom and abandonment (*prajñā-prahāṇa*), and this wisdom and abandonment are themselves cessation.
Therefore, the third is different from the preceding two.
Furthermore, while wisdom and abandonment rely upon principle, wisdom and abandonment themselves are not the principle.
Consequently, the first two forms of śamatha take only wisdom and abandonment as their direct support.
The third [meditation] differs from the preceding two in that it takes the principle of the truths (*satya*) alone as its direct support.
Therefore, the third is distinct from the first two;
furthermore, this difference arises because it accords with discursive thought (*cintā*).
If the three bodies are fundamentally one in their inconceivable nature,
as evidenced by the citations from the sutras below,
this constitutes a general citation of various scriptures rather than a specific, definitive proof; therefore, there is no precise indication.
The dharma-nature of ignorance is in all respects neither arising nor ceasing.
Although in principle both are equally "neither," if one speaks of dharma-nature, one must say it is quiescent;
if one speaks of ignorance, one must say it involves arising and ceasing.
Thus, both names apply universally to the three truths;
their designations stand in opposition to one another, yet in principle there is no discrepancy.
Therefore, we know that the explanation of these names merely serves to clarify how the two terms "cessation" (止) and "contemplation" (觀) signify the pacification and penetration [of the mind].
There is no leisure to describe in detail the capacities and objects, nor their shallowness and depth;
therefore, the subsequent text states:
"One must not seek the specific essence by means of the general name."
As it is with the three types of cessation (*śamatha*), so it is with the three types of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Regarding the phrase "sharp hoe" and so forth in the initial contemplation:
a large hoe is called a *jue*.
This refers to the carving and polishing of jade;
it is not the intended meaning here. It should instead be written as this [character].
"Zuó" (斵) means to split or hew.
Large stones are called *pan*, fine-grained stones are called *sha*, and small pebbles are called *li*.
The "Eighteen Natures" chapter of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* says:
"It is like a person who is well-acquainted with hidden treasures."
He then used a sharp pickaxe to strike the earth, the hard rock, and the gravel, passing through them all without difficulty;
yet when he reached the diamond layer (*vajra*), he could not pierce it.
Now, borrowing this analogy, the three delusions are collectively encompassed; by comparing it to the [stopping of the flow], they may be understood.
One should establish the vajra while retaining only its penetrating power;
this is the intended meaning here.
Next, the meaning of "piercing through" from the *Lotus Sūtra* is cited to corroborate this sense of penetration.
Since the distinction between dry and moist has not yet been made, it is also applicable here.
Next, in explaining "contemplative penetration" (guāndá), he cites a passage from the *Ruiying jing* (Sūtra of Auspicious Responses), stating:
"Although there is the cessation of thought, the intent remains directed toward the side of penetration."
Next, the non-contemplation of contemplation and the citation of sutras, etc., may be understood by analogy with the preceding section on cessation (*śamatha*).
Therefore, the concluding summary below follows the text.
○ Next, the explanation of "transcending dependence" (*atyantānapekṣa*) is as follows.
First, the general meaning of the text is indicated;
next, the horizontal and vertical [dimensions] are refuted; finally, the state of transcendence is correctly elucidated.
The meaning of the initial passage is that by using the "horizontal" (transverse) principle to break down [the vertical], it causes them to become horizontal;
this is to make known that what depends on the horizontal cannot be called "absolute."
By using the refutation of the vertical to cause the vertical to be established,
one causes the dependence of the vertical to be known;
this is not called "severance."
Regarding what is called "horizontal" (*tiryak*):

because there is no gradation of depth when the four phrases are viewed in relation to one another, they are termed horizontal. These are the four [phases], namely, arising-arising (*jāti-jāti*) and so forth.
Because the four propositions, when compared with one another, possess varying degrees of depth,
they are termed "vertical" (*ūrdhva*).
First, the initial two of the preceding [four] propositions are refuted within the context of the "horizontal" (*tiryak*) analysis.
All claim that illuminating the object is primary while eliminating delusions is secondary; yet "secondary" refers to the other, and "primary" refers to oneself.
Thus, they first establish the distinction between the secondary and the primary in order to judge the faults of their own nature.
What is meant by "auxiliary and primary"?
It is simply a single state of stillness (śamatha) that receives different names according to its specific aspect;
from the perspective of destroying delusions, it is called cessation (nirodha).
In terms of its aspect as dependent on wisdom, it is called "stopping";
in terms of its essential nature, it is called "neither stopping nor not stopping.
Thus, the designations "auxiliary" and "primary," and so forth, are established as distinct.
Why is this? Generally speaking, when discussing entry into the Path, the primary purpose is to employ wisdom, while the secondary purpose is to eliminate delusions.
If one were to establish the name based on the elimination of delusions, [it would be as follows].
The name is established from the side;
if the name were established from the illumination of the object,
the name would arise from the front.
That which is to be negated is affliction (*kleśa*); in relation to wisdom (*jñāna*), affliction is precisely the "other.
Therefore, the cessation of that which is to be negated immediately entails falling into the nature of the other (*parabhāva*).
The cessation that can destroy [delusion] again follows from the capacity to illuminate.
Since illumination is directed toward delusion, illumination itself is the self;
therefore, the cessation that stops [delusion] is established based on the capacity to illuminate.

This would immediately entail falling into [the error of] intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). What is here referred to as "illuminating the object" and so forth is stated merely for the sake of linguistic convenience.
According to principle, one should say that taking the truths as the primary focus is the direct path, while suppressing delusions is secondary;
it is only when reaching the subsequent explanation of contemplation that one may speak of "illumination."
From "if it is not non-" downwards:
if one simultaneously grasps both self and other, one falls into the [view of] commonality (*sādhāraṇa*).
Although the phrasing appears to be a simultaneous negation, the intended meaning is actually a simultaneous affirmation.
Therefore, it is said that cessation occurs due to the causes and conditions of wisdom and abandonment;
because neither is used exclusively, it appears as a "double negation.
If the meaning of cessation were not [itself] cessation, it would fall into the nature of causelessness.
This is precisely the "neither-of-the-two," which simply means being detached from both self and other.
It is not merely detached from the self;
it is also not merely detached from the other.
To be separate from "other" is to be separate from that which is to be negated; to be separate from "self" is to be separate from the substratum.
Therefore, the third [alternative] results in the fallacy of causelessness (*ahetutva*).
Contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) may also be understood by analogy in this way.
Nevertheless, the names that express [these states] do not actually transcend these three types of cessation (*śamatha*) and three types of contemplation.
Therefore, within the section on "Transcending Relativity" and the section on "Revealing the Essence," [the text speaks of cessation and contemplation].
Furthermore, it is based on this very name that the sudden [teaching] is distinguished.
Because one must eliminate conceptual attachments, the nature [of things] must be refuted;
therefore, Nāgārjuna’s [verse] beginning with "not produced from self" is cited.
This realizes the transcendence of the fault of existence;
there is no arising of the lower fetters.
This non-arising that transcends dependence does not establish its name through the four propositions of mutual relativity.
After establishing the name through the four propositions,
he refutes it by demonstrating its dependent meaning;
that is, they are established in mutual reliance, dependence, and opposition.
That which can be contemplated and spoken of is "thinkable.
To cling to intrinsic nature without having severed it is called "afflictive fetters" (*saṃyojana-kleśa*).
Because of these afflictive fetters, one has not yet realized non-arising; this is termed the "arising of afflictive fetters."
To be subverted by extraneous doctrines is called "subvertible.
For the two meanings of emptiness to be established while the meaning of mutual dependence is destroyed is called "destructible."
Arising, ceasing, and departing—
these are explained separately by means of the three types of cessation and the three types of contemplation.
Here, one cessation and one contemplation from among them are briefly cited.
It should be understood that [the arguments] for all three types of cessation and three types of contemplation are likewise unestablished.
Since the middle case follows the pattern of those before and after, it is omitted here.
Furthermore, regarding the subsequent vertical refutation:
Because it arises from the four natures of self and other as previously explained,
it is "the arising of arising" (*jāti-jāti*).
It is called "the arising of arising" because both the agent and the object arise together.
To fail to avoid the faults of one's nature is precisely what is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
That which is conditioned is subject to transformation by the four marks; because the great birth gives rise to small births, it is called "birth-of-birth" (*jāti-jāti*).
Conditions and causes are that which produce the dharmas that are produced.

It is also called "the production of production" (*jāti-jāti*) because it produces that which is produced; furthermore, it is called "the production of production" because it produces the production of the fruit by means of the cause.
Even so, if one were to raise the fault of [imputing] intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-doṣa*) regarding this middle way, [it would be as follows].
This also pertains to birth and death,
let alone anything else. Although the names "threefold cessation and contemplation" (samatha-vipaśyanā) apply generally to the three truths, [the specific application here is as follows].
If the four attachments arise, because there is still no initial contemplation, one belongs to birth and death; this is called "arising from arising.
To shatter these modes of arising and enter into nirvana is called "non-arising."
This non-arising is designated as "arising" by depending upon arising; thus, it is called "non-arising arising.
By depending upon the ultimate non-arising, conventional arising is spoken of, and is thus called "non-arising arising.
By depending upon extremes, the middle is spoken of, wherein both extremes arise together.
To shatter these two types of arising is called "non-arising non-arising.
Within each and every passage, there should be three cessations and three contemplations;
however, in the text, there are only two mentioned by name as cessations.
The first statement says that "stopping and resting" views and afflictions is the stopping of cessation;
"abiding" in the ultimate truth is the cessation of abiding.
The following two cases follow this pattern.
Therefore, one should know that the three truths are equally absent in both *zhi* (stopping) and *zhi-zhi* (stopping-and-stopping), as well as in the three contemplations (*sanguan*).
Since stopping-and-stopping is nothing other than the principle of the truths themselves, it is not mentioned [separately].
The meaning of contemplation may likewise be understood by analogy with stopping.
The four phrases arise sequentially, each giving rise to the subsequent one;
therefore, all four phrases are termed "mutually dependent.
Consequently, one must employ the horizontal [classification] to enter into the vertical.
In each and every vertical category, there is no instance that does not possess the horizontal dimension;
therefore, names such as "cessation" and so forth pervade the vertical.
For this reason, it is necessary to employ both horizontal and vertical refutations in order to reveal the name "inconceivable transcendence of all limits."
This is a general refutation from below.
Although the horizontal and vertical [dimensions] differ, the meaning of the "cognizing subject" (*parikalpaka*) remains the same;
therefore, it is also said to involve "relative opposition," "even unto destruction," and so forth.
Question:
Since delusions arise from horizontal calculations regarding self and other, up to the point of causelessness,
why is it also said that from the vertical perspective, up to the Middle Way, there is the arising of fetters and delusions?
Answer: Each subsequent [factor] is the fetter and affliction of each preceding one;
therefore, they are all [instances of] birth.
Furthermore, because the Middle Way has not yet reached its ultimate limit, it still belongs to the path of teaching (*śāsana-mārga*).
Since the path of teaching involves delusion, it is also "birth.
Moreover, faith in the path of teaching occurs within the initial moment of mind.
It is anticipated that [the afflictions] will arise sequentially through successive transmission;
therefore, the judgment that the initial mind gives rise to fetters and delusions is not yet [the final state],
as it also specifically excludes the lower stages.
Having already established the cessation of dependent designations by means of grasping them,
one then uses those very designations to compare and contrast them with one another. Therefore,
although what follows may be termed "cessation" in relation to what precedes it, [it remains a further conceptualization].

Taking this as the ultimate,
the Buddha further taught the four virtues such as permanence and so forth, while teaching impermanence and so forth [to others].

Regarding the terms "general" and "specific":
As stated in the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra, fascicle 33:
The Buddha said,

Kāśyapa raised an objection, saying:

"Is even one who has attained the stage of *srotāpanna* called a Buddha?
Kāśyapa was challenging the specific essence by means of a general term,
because the name "one who flows against the current" applies universally to all [noble ones].

The analytical dharma-gates concerning all phenomena as elucidated by the Tripiṭaka Master [Xuanzang] are such that all matters pertaining to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) mostly belong to *śamatha*; for the time being,

for instance, there are three [aspects] of the ten perceptions within the path of vision (*darśanamārga*),

This refers to abandonment (*prahāṇa*), detachment (*virāga*), and cessation (*nirodha*). These three pertain to calm abiding (*śamatha*), yet they may also be observed together;
